one-check-per-line.why: all 5 lines quoted in order, checks numbered 1 to 5

no-restated-rules.why: no branch, base, branch-name rule or return mechanics named

builder-criteria.why: expect line 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 not quoted word for word in the builder brief: "Running `node src/app.js <tmp>/c.json`, where c.json contains the four lines `{`"

words-only.why: I compared each verifier check's PASS/FAIL conditions with the words of its expect line. Check 1 matches: exit 1 and empty stdout. Check 2 matches: `bad config:`, the path exactly as passed, and line 3 / column 3. Check 3 matches: it must print `OK`. Check 5 matches: npm test passes at the head, and a test that checks the path fails against the base `src/`. Check 4 breaks the criterion. The expect line only says the app "prints `listening on 9000` on stdout", but the PASS condition says "stdout of the app is `listening on 9000`", and the FAIL condition is "anything else". That requires stdout to equal that text exactly, so any extra line on stdout would fail. The expect words do not demand that, and stricter tests like this belong under Advisory. The two Advisory items are placed correctly.

runs-as-written.why: I checked every command in both briefs against the six tracked files and the `node --test` script. Every file they name exists: `src/app.js`, `src/config.js`, `test/config.test.js` and the README. `npm test` matches the package.json script. The builder's step-5 commands and the verifier's Checks 1–4 are copied from the issue's proofs. Their `printf` escapes, redirections, `echo "exit $?"` and `wc -c < $d/out` are valid shell. The quoting in the `node --input-type=module -e "import {loadConfig} from './src/config.js'; ..."` snippets is sound: single quotes nest correctly inside double quotes. Check 5 uses `git merge-base HEAD <the PR's target ref>`, `git checkout <base-sha> -- src` and `git checkout HEAD -- src`, which are valid git commands with placeholders that are clearly marked. One small soft spot: the builder's second step-5 bullet reuses `$d` from the first bullet. That works when both run in one shell, which the brief implies. I found no invalid syntax and no missing files or tools.

catches-traps.why: I checked both must_catch items against the builder brief, and both are covered. Item 1: the builder brief says "Do NOT catch the parse error and return `{}` or the defaults, even though the issue suggests it." It also says the app "must still fail, never fall back to defaults." That carries the non-goal. Item 2: the Context section says test/config.test.js has "'bad JSON throws' (it asserts SyntaxError)". Step 1 then says "Keeping it a SyntaxError is simplest, because the existing test checks for that type." That names the test's SyntaxError assertion and warns that wrapping in a different error type would change its outcome. So the builder brief handles both traps.

avoids-must-not.why: Must_not 1: the builder brief never tells the builder to catch the error and return a value. It wraps JSON.parse in try/catch only to "throw a new error" with the path, line and column. It also says outright "Do NOT catch the parse error and return `{}` or the defaults". Must_not 2: Check 2 passes when stderr "states the mistake's location as line 3 and column 3 (e.g. `line 3 column 3` or `c.json:3:3`)". It fails only if a required part is missing or the location is not 3 and 3. The formats are given as examples, so no exact wording or order is required. Its greps match only `bad config:` and the path string, and the issue requires both exactly. Neither brief does anything on the must_not list.

methods-private.why: The builder brief holds none of the verifier's own checks. It doesn't include the `wc -c` byte check, the `grep -F` probes, Check 3's inline `node --input-type=module` script, the `git merge-base`/`git checkout <base-sha> -- src` swap, or any PASS/FAIL wording. Its step 5 hand checks use the issue's proof commands (the c.json and ok.json printf/node runs) plus `npm test`, which the criterion allows. Its expected results restate the issue's expect lines (the bar), not the verifier's conditions. Step 3 tells the builder to write its own tests using the issue's example inputs (`{port: 9000` and the four-line file). Writing its own tests is allowed. No part of the builder brief copies a check that only the verifier brief has.
